en: docker sandbox run clod can be very useful
for, well, running clod code in a sandbox.
But clod code also has a built-in sandbox
mode you can use as an alternative if you
don't have Docker or if you don't want to
use Docker or
because in that Docker sandbox certain
features might not work the way you want
them to work. For example, clod code using
the browser, a feature we'll dive in later.
I consistently had some problems with that.
And for all these reasons, you can use the
built-in sandbox mode by simply running
/sandbox inside of a Claude Code session.
This will then ask you which sandbox mode
you want to set up,
if you want to
use auto allow or with regular permissions.
And auto allow is what I want here because
the idea behind this Claude Code sandbox is
that it does scope the access of Claude Code
to this project folder
and that it also controls the network access
to prevent exfiltration of data that might
be stored in your project, for example.
So if I enable this, you'll see my settings
file will have been updated, or if you
didn't have a file yet, it will have been
created. And in there you have this sandbox
entry now. And of course you could have also
added it manually.
With that added,
all future Claude Code sessions you may
start will run in that sandbox mode. So you
could run Claude Code with dangerously
skip permissions. And since that sandbox
mode is enabled,
you'll not accidentally erase your overall
hard drive. As you also see here, I'm
running in the sandbox mode. And that of
course can therefore be a very useful mode
because it gives you a Claude Code
experience where you don't constantly
constantly have to grant permissions and at
the same time you have some safety and you
have that without using Docker, which
nonetheless would be a good alternative.
Now in this course, I'll actually not use
this dangerously-skip-permissions flag.
Instead, I'll run Claude Code like this and
explicitly grant permissions because I want
to see what Claude Code wants to do because
there are certain things I don't want it to
do, not because I'm afraid of losing my hard
drive, but because I see that it's the wrong
direction into which it's going. But that of
course comes down to personal preference.
And if you want a more hands-off approach,
using Sandbox and this dangerous permissions
mode can be a good way forward.
